item.research_question: How do new Ti-rich BCC high-entropy alloys designed using the Bo-Md approach deform, and do they exhibit transformation induced plasticity (TRIP) to achieve high strength and ductility?
item.processing_route: Vacuum arc melting to fabricate ingots; tensile specimens (4 mm length × 1 mm width × 0.8 mm thickness) cut from as-cast alloys; tensile tests at room temperature with a constant strain-rate of 10−3 s−1 until fracture
item.test_conditions: Room temperature; constant strain-rate of 10−3 s−1; microstructural analysis via EBSD and TEM on fractured specimens
key_findings: The alloy Ti38Zr25Hf25Ta10Sn2 showed the highest yield strength of 407 MPa and tensile strength of 925 MPa.
The alloy Ti35Zr27.5Hf27.5Nb5Ta5 showed a yield strength of 121 MPa and a tensile strength of 574 MPa.
The ratio of maximum tensile strength to yield strength was 2.2 for Ti38Zr25Hf25Ta10Sn2 and 4.7 for Ti35Zr27.5Hf27.5Nb5Ta5.
All alloys maintained high ductility with engineering plastic strain greater than 10%.
Microstructural observations confirmed the transformation of the BCC (β) matrix to HCP (α′) martensite during deformation.
The transformed α′ fraction was maximum in the Ti38Zr25Hf25Ta10Sn2 alloy, which exhibited the highest tensile strength and ductility.
Crystallographic analysis indicated a strong variant selection with (1 1 0)β//(0 0 0 1)α′ and [1 − 1 1]β//[1 1 − 2 0]α′.
Deformation twins were observed inside the transformed α′ phase in the Ti38Zr25Hf25Ta10Sn2 alloy.
item.mechanism: The authors explain the high strain-hardening and ductility through the TRIP effect, where the metastable soft β phase transforms into a relatively hard α′ phase. This transformation generates distinct phase boundaries that dynamically refine the effective grain size (dynamic Hall–Petch effect), decrease the mean free path for dislocation slip, and induce geometrically necessary dislocations (GNDs) to create long-range stress fields. Additionally, the transformed α′ phase deforms by twinning or dislocation slip, and the specific Burgers orientation relationship ensures a low-energy interface that facilitates the transformation.
item.limitations: The text notes that the yield strength of the Ti35Zr27.5Hf27.5Nb5Ta5 alloy in this study (121 MPa) was significantly lower than a previously reported value (540 MPa) due to the coarse initial grain size (d ~ 220 µm) compared to the previous study (d ~ 40 µm).
item.future_work: Controlling the microstructure, especially decreasing the initial grain size using appropriate thermo-mechanical processing route, might result in a remarkable increment of strength and ductility; further optimization of microstructural parameters is being done and will be reported in a future article.
quotes: The alloys showed exceptionally high strain-hardening and ductility.
Post-deformation microstructural observations confirmed the transformation of β to hexagonal close packed (HCP, α′) martensite.
The transformed α′ having high hardness values compared to the β phase was previously reported.

Question: How do new Ti-rich BCC high-entropy alloys designed using the Bo-Md approach deform, and do they exhibit transformation induced plasticity (TRIP) to achieve high strength and ductility?. System: Ti35Zr27.5Hf27.5Nb5Ta5, Ti38Zr25Hf25Ta10Sn2, and Ti38Zr25Hf25Ta7Sn5 (in at%). Processing: Vacuum arc melting to fabricate ingots; tensile specimens (4 mm length × 1 mm width × 0.8 mm thickness) cut from as-cast alloys; tensile tests at room temperature with a constant strain-rate of 10−3 s−1 until fracture. Test conditions: Room temperature; constant strain-rate of 10−3 s−1; microstructural analysis via EBSD and TEM on fractured specimens. Findings: The alloy Ti38Zr25Hf25Ta10Sn2 showed the highest yield strength of 407 MPa and tensile strength of 925 MPa.; The alloy Ti35Zr27.5Hf27.5Nb5Ta5 showed a yield strength of 121 MPa and a tensile strength of 574 MPa.; The ratio of maximum tensile strength to yield strength was 2.2 for Ti38Zr25Hf25Ta10Sn2 and 4.7 for Ti35Zr27.5Hf27.5Nb5Ta5.; All alloys maintained high ductility with engineering plastic strain greater than 10%.; Microstructural observations confirmed the transformation of the BCC (β) matrix to HCP (α′) martensite during deformation.; The transformed α′ fraction was maximum in the Ti38Zr25Hf25Ta10Sn2 alloy, which exhibited the highest tensile strength and ductility.; Crystallographic analysis indicated a strong variant selection with (1 1 0)β//(0 0 0 1)α′ and [1 − 1 1]β//[1 1 − 2 0]α′.; Deformation twins were observed inside the transformed α′ phase in the Ti38Zr25Hf25Ta10Sn2 alloy.. Mechanism: The authors explain the high strain-hardening and ductility through the TRIP effect, where the metastable soft β phase transforms into a relatively hard α′ phase. This transformation generates distinct phase boundaries that dynamically refine the effective grain size (dynamic Hall–Petch effect), decrease the mean free path for dislocation slip, and induce geometrically necessary dislocations (GNDs) to create long-range stress fields. Additionally, the transformed α′ phase deforms by twinning or dislocation slip, and the specific Burgers orientation relationship ensures a low-energy interface that facilitates the transformation.. Limitations: The text notes that the yield strength of the Ti35Zr27.5Hf27.5Nb5Ta5 alloy in this study (121 MPa) was significantly lower than a previously reported value (540 MPa) due to the coarse initial grain size (d ~ 220 µm) compared to the previous study (d ~ 40 µm).. Future work: Controlling the microstructure, especially decreasing the initial grain size using appropriate thermo-mechanical processing route, might result in a remarkable increment of strength and ductility; further optimization of microstructural parameters is being done and will be reported in a future article..
